title: Layout With Flow, Flexbox, and Grid
summary: Place boxes on the page with normal flow, positioning, Flexbox for rows and columns, and Grid for layouts that line up both ways.
intro: Colors and fonts are the easy part of CSS. Most of the time you spend on a page goes into **layout**: where each box goes. A sidebar that drops below the content, a menu hidden behind the page, buttons that won't sit in a row, a footer floating halfway up a short page: each of these is a layout problem. This lesson starts with what the browser does when you say nothing, called normal flow. Then it covers taking a box out of the flow to pin it somewhere, Flexbox for lining boxes up in a row or a column, and Grid for rows and columns at once. The last part shows how to choose between them, with patterns you'll use on almost every site. The examples now move from the bakery to Trail Guide, a site for finding hiking trails, with far more to lay out.

steps.title: Normal flow: where boxes go by default
steps.body:
Every layout starts from what the browser does before you change anything. That default is called **normal flow**, and most of any page stays in it: the text of an article, a list, a form. Knowing it well saves you from reaching for a bigger tool when the default already does the job.

## Block and inline

The previous lesson showed that every element is a box, with content, padding, a border, and a margin, and the lesson on HTML documents sorted elements into block and inline ones. In normal flow, a box's kind decides where it goes.

- A **block** box starts on a new line and stretches across the whole width of the box it's in. The next box goes below it. Headings, paragraphs, lists, `section`, and `div` (the element that means nothing and only groups others) are block boxes.
- An **inline** box sits inside a line of text, the way a word does. It's only as wide as its content, the next one follows it on the same line, and when the line is full they carry on to the next line. Links, `strong`, `em`, `span`, and `img` are inline.

```diagram flow-flexbox-and-grid-normal-flow
Blocks stack down the page. Inline boxes run along the lines inside a block.
```

In the diagram, the heading, the paragraph, and the list are blocks, so each takes a full row and they stack down the page. Inside the paragraph, the words, the bold word, and the link are inline: they run along the line and wrap onto the next one. Blocks go down and inline boxes go across, the same way you read a page of English.

## Changing a box's kind with display

Every element gets its kind from the browser's own stylesheet, and the `display` property changes it. These are the values you'll use, besides `flex` and `grid`, which have parts of their own:

| Value | What the box does |
|---|---|
| `block` | starts a new line and fills the width |
| `inline` | flows along the line, and ignores `width` and `height` |
| `inline-block` | flows along the line like a word, but takes a width, a height, and padding like a block |
| `flow-root` | a block that always contains everything inside it |
| `none` | isn't drawn at all, and takes up no space |

`display: none` takes the element out of the page completely, as if it weren't in the HTML, and screen readers skip it too. To hide something but keep its space, use `visibility: hidden`.

`flow-root` fixes two old surprises. The first is **floats**: `float: left` on a picture lets the text beside it wrap around it, like a photo in a magazine, and that's the one job floats still have. A floated picture taller than the text next to it sticks out of the bottom of its parent, and `display: flow-root` on the parent makes it grow to hold the picture. The second is margins: it stops a child's top margin from escaping through its parent's top edge, which is the margin collapsing you met with the box model.

## How wide is a box?

A block fills the width it's given, and grows as tall as its content. You can also size a box by what's inside it, with three keywords called **intrinsic sizes**:

- `min-content` is the narrowest the box can be without anything sticking out, usually the width of its longest word.
- `max-content` is as wide as the content wants to be if nothing wraps.
- `fit-content` is `max-content`, but never wider than the space there is. Past that, the text wraps.

`width: fit-content` is the handy one. It makes a block shrink to fit its text, while still starting on its own line.

## When content doesn't fit

Give a box a fixed size and put too much in it, and the extra spills out over whatever comes next. That's `overflow: visible`, the default: the browser would rather show your content in the wrong place than hide it from someone. The `overflow` property picks something else:

- `auto` adds a scrollbar only when the content doesn't fit. It's the one you'll want most often.
- `scroll` always shows scrollbars, even with nothing to scroll.
- `hidden` cuts off what doesn't fit, with no scrollbar.
- `clip` cuts it off too, and makes sure nothing can scroll it into view.

A box with `auto`, `scroll`, or `hidden` becomes a **scroll container**: its content scrolls inside it while the rest of the page stays still. `overflow-x` and `overflow-y` set one direction at a time. That's how you keep a wide table or a long line of code from making the whole page scroll sideways on a phone: wrap it in a box with `overflow-x: auto`, and only that box scrolls.

One more spill to know: a long word with no spaces, like a web address, can't wrap, so it pokes out of a narrow box. `overflow-wrap: anywhere` lets the browser break it wherever it has to.

examples.title: Block and inline boxes, outlined
examples.prompt: A page with a heading, a paragraph with a link in it, and a short list. The outline shows where each box is, without changing its size.
examples.code:
Trail notes

Start at the north gate and follow the map to the lake.

  • Bring water
  • Wear good shoes
examples.explanation: The `*` selector picks every element, and `outline` draws a line around each box without taking up any space, unlike a border. Open the page and the red lines show normal flow at work. The `h1`, the `p`, the `ul`, and each `li` stretch across the whole window, one below another, even though their text is short: block boxes fill the width they're given. Inside the paragraph, the `strong` and the `a` get small outlines that hug their words, since inline boxes are only as wide as their content. Make the window narrow and the paragraph's line breaks before the link, and the link's outline wraps onto two lines with it. An outline like this is a quick way to see the boxes on any page you're working on, and DevTools shows the same when you hover over an element in its Elements panel.

examples.title: A tag that fits its text
examples.prompt: Two ways to make a label shrink to its text, for a small tag like New above a product's name.
examples.explanation: The `.tag` rule makes an inline box that behaves like a block on the inside. It still sits in a line of text like a word, so two tags go side by side, but its padding now pushes the lines around it apart, as a block's would. A plain inline box draws vertical padding without making room for it, so it would overlap the lines above and below. A `border-radius` larger than half the height, like `999px`, rounds the ends fully into a pill shape. The `.notice` rule keeps a block, so it still starts on its own line, but `width: fit-content` shrinks it to its text, and its border hugs the words instead of running across the whole page. `currentColor` is the element's own text color, so the border always matches it.

examples.title: A table that scrolls on its own
examples.prompt: A wide table in a box that scrolls sideways, so the rest of the page fits a phone's screen.
examples.code:
TrailLengthClimbSurfaceDogs
North Loop8 km310 mgravelon a lead
examples.explanation: The table has five columns and `min-width: 40rem` keeps them readable, so on a phone it's wider than the screen. Without the wrapper, the whole page would scroll sideways, and the reader would keep losing the text. The `div` has `overflow-x: auto`, which makes it a scroll container: the table scrolls left and right inside it, and everything else stays put. On a wide screen the table fits, so no scrollbar appears at all. That's the difference between `auto` and `scroll`, which would show an empty scrollbar even then. Code blocks get the same treatment: this lesson's own code boxes scroll sideways when a line is too long for your screen.

steps.title: Positioning, and what sits on top
steps.body:
Some things have to break out of normal flow: the red number on the corner of a cart icon, a header that stays at the top while you scroll, a dialog that covers the page. The `position` property takes a box out of its usual place, and once boxes overlap, you need to know how the browser decides which one is in front.

## The five positions

- `static` is the default: the box sits in normal flow, and `top`, `right`, `bottom`, and `left` do nothing.
- `relative` keeps the box in the flow, and its space with it, but lets `top` and `left` nudge where it's drawn. Its main use is a side effect, explained next: it becomes the box its `absolute` children are placed against.
- `absolute` takes the box out of the flow. The boxes around it close up as if it weren't there, and it's placed with `top`, `right`, `bottom`, and `left`, measured from the edges of its containing block.
- `fixed` is like `absolute`, but measured from the viewport, the part of the browser window that shows the page. It stays in place on the screen when you scroll.
- `sticky` stays in the flow and scrolls like normal until it reaches the edge you set, like `top: 0`, then sticks there while its parent is still on screen.

`inset` sets all four sides at once, so `inset: 0` stretches a box to all four edges of its containing block.

## The containing block

An `absolute` box is placed against its **containing block**: the nearest ancestor (a box it's inside, at any depth) whose `position` isn't `static`. That's why you'll see `position: relative` on a box with no offsets at all. It's there to say: place my `absolute` children against me. Leave it off, and the browser keeps looking up the tree, and a badge meant for a button's corner ends up in the corner of the page.

## Sticky's two traps

A sticky header that won't stick is nearly always one of two things. It needs an edge to stick at, so `position: sticky` with no `top` does nothing. And it sticks inside the nearest box that scrolls, so an ancestor with `overflow: hidden` or `auto` (a scroll container, from the previous part) traps it there, and it scrolls away with the page. A sticky box also stops at the end of its parent, which is what you want for a heading that sticks while its own section is on screen.

## Who's in front

When boxes overlap, the browser paints them in order: boxes in normal flow first, then positioned boxes on top, each group in the order they come in the HTML. `z-index` changes the order: a positioned box with a higher `z-index` is drawn in front of one with a lower one.

The surprise is that `z-index` numbers only compete inside a group. A **stacking context** is a group of boxes that's painted together, as one layer, and the whole layer sits at one spot in its parent's order. A box with `z-index: 9999` inside a header whose own `z-index` is 1 can never rise above a box beside that header with `z-index: 2`. The 9999 only beats the header's other children.

```diagram flow-flexbox-and-grid-stacking
The menu's 9999 only counts inside the header. The header, at 1, sits under main, at 2.
```

In the diagram, the page holds two stacking contexts side by side. The header's is at level 1, and main's is at level 2, so all of main is painted after all of the header. The menu belongs to the header's group, so it's painted with the header and ends up under main, however big its number is.

These things create a stacking context, so it's worth knowing them when a `z-index` doesn't work:

- a positioned box with a `z-index` other than `auto`
- `position: fixed` or `sticky`
- `opacity` below 1, a `transform`, or a `filter`
- `isolation: isolate`, which exists only to make one

The fix is to raise the group, not the child: give the header a higher `z-index` than main. Teams also keep a short list of `z-index` values in custom properties, like `--z-header: 10` and `--z-overlay: 100`, so numbers don't creep up into the thousands.

## The top layer

Dialogs and pop-ups have a better way. A `dialog` opened as a modal, and an element with the `popover` attribute, both from the HTML lessons, are drawn in the browser's **top layer**, above every stacking context on the page, with no `z-index` at all. When you build something that covers the page, reach for those first.

examples.title: A badge on a button's corner
examples.prompt: A cart button with the number of items pinned to its top right corner.
examples.explanation: `position: relative` on the button doesn't move it at all. It makes the button the containing block for the badge. The badge is `absolute`, so it leaves the flow, and the button shrinks to fit only the word Cart, as if the badge weren't inside it. Then `top: -0.5rem` and `right: -0.5rem` put the badge's top and right edges half a rem outside the button's, so it hangs over the corner the way badges usually do. `min-width` keeps a one-digit badge round, and a two-digit one grows wider. Take `position: relative` off the button, and the badge flies to the top right corner of the page, since no ancestor is positioned and the browser falls back to the top of the page.

examples.title: A header that sticks while you scroll
examples.prompt: A site header that scrolls with the page until it reaches the top of the window, then stays there.
examples.explanation: `position: sticky` with `top: 0` keeps the header in normal flow, so it takes up its space at the top of the page and pushes the content below it. When you scroll and its top edge reaches the top of the window, it stops there and the page slides under it. The background matters: a header has a transparent background by default, so without one, the text scrolling underneath would show through it. `z-index: 10` keeps it above positioned boxes further down the page, like the cart badge, which would otherwise be painted on top of it as they scroll past. If it still won't stick, look for an ancestor with `overflow` set: that's the most common reason.

examples.title: A menu that hides behind the page
examples.prompt: A dropdown menu inside the header, and a main area below it. The menu's z-index is far higher, and it's still covered.
examples.code:
Trail Guide
  • Trails
  • Maps
Popular this week
examples.explanation: `top: 100%` places the menu just below the header, so it hangs down over main. It looks like 9999 should win, but the header has a position and a `z-index`, so it's a stacking context, and the menu's number only counts inside it. Main, at 2, is painted after the whole header group, at 1, and its white background covers the menu. You'll find this exact bug on real sites, often after someone adds a `z-index` to a section for some other reason. Changing the header to `z-index: 3` fixes it, and so does removing main's `z-index`, since then main makes no group and paints below the header's.

steps.title: Flexbox: a row or a column of boxes
steps.body:
Putting boxes side by side is the most common layout job there is: a logo on the left and links on the right, three buttons in a row, an icon next to its label. Normal flow can't do it well, since blocks stack and inline boxes only line up like words. **Flexbox**, short for flexible box layout, lays boxes out in one line, a row or a column, and decides how they share the space.

## Containers and items

Put `display: flex` on a box, and it becomes a **flex container**. Its children, and only its direct children, become **flex items**. They line up in a row, each as wide as its content, and all as tall as the tallest one. Anything inside an item goes back to normal flow, so a paragraph in a flex item still works like a paragraph.

## Two axes

Flexbox thinks in two directions. The **main axis** is the way the items go, and `flex-direction` sets it: `row`, the default, runs along the line like text, and `column` runs down the page. The **cross axis** runs across it. Every alignment property works along one of the two:

```diagram flow-flexbox-and-grid-flex-axes
In a row, the main axis runs across and the cross axis runs down. justify-content works along the first, align-items along the second.
```

- `justify-content` places the items along the main axis: `flex-start` (the default), `center`, `flex-end`, `space-between` (the first at the start, the last at the end, and equal gaps between), or `space-evenly` (equal gaps everywhere).
- `align-items` places them along the cross axis: `stretch` (the default, which makes them all as tall as the row), `center`, `flex-start`, `flex-end`, or `baseline`, which lines up the bottoms of their first lines of text.
- `align-self` on one item overrides `align-items` for that item alone.
- `gap` puts space between the items, and never before the first or after the last.

With `flex-direction: column`, the axes swap. Now `justify-content` works up and down and `align-items` works left and right. When an alignment does the opposite of what you expected, check the direction first.

## Sharing the space

Each item starts at a size called its **flex basis**, usually the size of its content. If the row has space left over, items can grow into it, and if it's too short, they can shrink. The `flex` property on an item says how, and four values cover almost everything:

| Value | Means | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `flex: 1` | start from zero and share the space equally | columns of equal width |
| `flex: auto` | start from the content's size, then grow or shrink | items that should fill the row but keep their natural sizes |
| `flex: none` | stay at the content's size | buttons and icons |
| `flex: 0 0 16rem` | exactly 16rem, no more, no less | a sidebar of fixed width |

The full form has three numbers: how much it grows, how much it shrinks, and the basis. `flex: 1` is short for `1 1 0`.

Two tricks come up all the time. An **auto margin** takes all the free space on its side, so `margin-inline-start: auto` on the last link in a header pushes it, and anything after it, to the far end. (`margin-inline-start` is the left margin in English, explained in the last part of this lesson.) And an item won't shrink smaller than its content by default, so a long word or a long file name makes it overflow the row. `min-width: 0` on the item lets it shrink, and then the text can wrap or be cut off.

## Wrapping

By default, all the items stay on one line and shrink to fit, however many there are. `flex-wrap: wrap` lets them carry on to a new line instead, like a row of tags or filter buttons. Each line is laid out on its own, so the items on one line don't line up in columns with the ones above. When you need them to, that's a grid.

examples.title: A header with a logo and links
examples.prompt: The logo sits on the left, the links on the right, and everything is centered vertically, whatever its height.
examples.code:
Trail Guide
Trails Maps About
examples.explanation: The header is a flex container with two items: the logo link and the `nav`. `align-items: center` centers them on the cross axis, so a big logo and small links line up through their middles instead of along the top. `gap: 1rem` keeps them apart. The `nav` has `margin-inline-start: auto`, an auto margin on its left side in English, which swallows all the free space in the row and pushes the `nav` to the right edge. The `nav` is a flex container too, with its own `gap`, so the three links sit in a row of their own. Flex containers nest freely like this, and most headers you'll build look a lot like this one.

examples.title: A search field that takes the rest of the row
examples.prompt: A text field and a button on one line. The button keeps its size and the field fills the rest.
examples.code:
<form class="search" action="/search">
  <input type="search" name="q" aria-label="Search trails">
  <button>Search</button>
</form>

<style>
  .search {
    display: flex;
    gap: 0.5rem;
  }

  .search input {
    flex: 1;
    min-width: 0;
  }
</style>
examples.explanation: `flex: 1` on the field means: start from zero and take all the space that's left. The button has no `flex` value, so it keeps its natural size, and the field grows or shrinks with the window around it. Without `flex: 1`, the field would stay at the browser's default width, about 20 characters, and leave a gap at the end of the row. `min-width: 0` matters on narrow screens: a text field has a built-in minimum width, and without this line it refuses to shrink, so on a small phone it pushes the button off the edge. `aria-label` names the field for screen readers, since there's no visible label.

examples.title: Tags that wrap onto new lines
examples.prompt: A list of tags that sit in a row, carry on to a new line when the row is full, and keep even gaps both ways.
examples.explanation: This styles a `ul` with the class `tags`. `list-style: none` and `padding: 0` take away the bullets and the indent a list has by default, so the tags line up with the text around them. `flex-wrap: wrap` lets the tags carry on to the next line when the row runs out of room, instead of squeezing them all into one row. `gap: 0.5rem` spaces them evenly, between items on a line and between the lines too. Each tag keeps its natural width, so the lines end at different places, and that's fine for tags. Because each line is laid out on its own, nothing lines up in columns, and that's the sign to switch to Grid when you need neat columns.

steps.title: Grid: rows and columns at once

examples.title: A page drawn with named areas
examples.prompt: A page with a header, a sidebar, main content, and a footer. The HTML is a header, an aside, a main, and a footer, in that order.
examples.explanation: The strings draw the layout as a picture: the header and the footer span both columns, and the sidebar and main share the middle row. The sidebar column is a fixed 16rem, and main takes the rest with `1fr`. The rows are `auto 1fr auto`: the header and the footer are as tall as their content, and the middle row takes all the height that's left. With `min-height: 100dvh`, the whole grid is at least as tall as the screen (`dvh`, from the CSS lessons, is a hundredth of the screen's height), so on a short page the footer still sits at the bottom instead of halfway up. The `>` in each selector means a direct child of `.page`, so a `header` inside an article elsewhere isn't affected.

examples.title: A card grid that picks its own columns
examples.prompt: A gallery of cards that shows as many columns as fit, from one on a phone to four or more on a wide screen.
examples.explanation: This styles a `ul` of cards. `repeat(auto-fit, ...)` fits as many columns as the width allows, each at least 15rem and stretched to share the row equally. Resize the window and the cards jump from four columns to three to two to one, with no rule written for any of those sizes. The `min(15rem, 100%)` inside is a guard for very narrow screens. On a phone narrower than 15rem plus its padding, a plain 15rem minimum would make the column wider than the screen and the page would scroll sideways. `min()` picks the smaller of its two values, so the floor becomes the full width there instead. It's a long line, but it's one you'll copy into nearly every project.

examples.title: Cards whose parts line up
examples.prompt: Each card holds a title, some text, and a button. Subgrid lines up those three parts across every card in a row.
examples.explanation: Each `.card` takes three rows of the outer grid with `grid-row: span 3`, one row for each of its parts. `grid-template-rows: subgrid` tells the card to lay its own children out on those outer rows instead of making rows of its own. So the row for titles is as tall as the longest title in the whole row of cards, and every card's text starts at the same height, and every button lines up along the bottom. Without subgrid, a card with a two-line title would push its button lower than its neighbors'. The card's own `gap` replaces the outer grid's row gap inside the card, so its parts can sit closer together than the cards themselves.

steps.title: Choosing a layout, and common patterns
steps.body:
You now have four ways to place boxes: normal flow, positioning, Flexbox, and Grid. Most layout struggles come from fighting the wrong one, like forcing a page of neat columns out of Flexbox. This part gives you the rule of thumb for choosing, the handful of patterns you'll build again and again, and the tools that show you what a layout is doing.

## One direction or two

- **Normal flow** is for text and most of a page: articles, forms, lists. Leave it alone when it works, since a column of paragraphs needs nothing else.
- **Flexbox** is for one direction, where the content decides the sizes: headers, toolbars, button rows, an icon beside its label, tags that wrap.
- **Grid** is for two directions, where the layout decides the sizes and the content fills it: page frames, galleries, a form with labels in one column and fields in another.
- **Positioning** is for things that float over the rest: badges, sticky bars, overlays.

They nest freely. A typical page is a grid, its header is a flex row, and the articles inside it are normal flow.

## Patterns you'll use everywhere

**Centering**, in both directions, is two lines with Grid. `place-items` sets the alignment on both axes at once:

```css
.center {
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
}
```

**A sidebar beside the content** is a grid with a fixed column and a flexible one, `grid-template-columns: 16rem 1fr`. On a phone there's no room for both, so it goes back to one column there. The next lesson shows how to change a layout at a given screen width.

**A card grid** is the `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(15rem, 100%), 1fr))` from the previous part, which picks its own number of columns.

**A header, the content, and a footer**, with the footer at the bottom even when the page is short, is a grid of three rows on the `body`, shown in the first example below.

## Logical properties

Everything so far has said left and right, but not every language is written that way. Arabic and Hebrew run from right to left, so on a page in those languages, the start of a line is its right edge. A `margin-left` meant to space a label from the start of its line ends up on the wrong side.

**Logical properties** name sides by the direction of the text instead. **Inline** is the direction a line of text runs, left to right in English. **Block** is the direction blocks stack, top to bottom. So:

| Logical | In English, means |
|---|---|
| `margin-inline-start` | `margin-left` |
| `padding-inline` | `padding-left` and `padding-right` |
| `padding-block` | `padding-top` and `padding-bottom` |
| `inset-inline-end` | `right` |
| `inline-size` | `width` |
| `block-size` | `height` |

Set `dir="rtl"` on a page in Arabic, and every logical property flips to the right side by itself. Flexbox and Grid already work this way: `flex-start` and the first grid column are on the right in a right-to-left page. Many teams now write logical properties by default, so a translated site needs no second stylesheet.

## Seeing a layout in DevTools

When a layout misbehaves, look at it before you change anything. In Chrome's DevTools, the Elements panel shows a small **grid** or **flex** badge next to every element that's a grid or flex container. Click the badge, and DevTools draws the layout over the page: the grid's lines with their numbers, its gaps and area names, or the flex items and the free space between them. The **Layout** tab lists every grid on the page, with switches for line numbers and area names. Firefox and Safari have the same tools.

Hover over an element in the Elements panel, too, and the page shades its content, padding, border, and margin in different colors. Between the badges and that shading, most layout bugs show themselves: a gap that's really a margin, a column that's narrower than you thought, an item that isn't a child of the container you styled.

examples.title: A footer that stays at the bottom
examples.prompt: The body holds a header, a main, and a footer. On a short page, the footer still sits at the bottom of the screen.
examples.explanation: The body becomes a grid with three rows, one for each of its children. The header and footer rows are `auto`, as tall as their content, and the middle row, main's, is `1fr`, so it takes whatever height is left. `min-height: 100dvh` makes the body at least as tall as the screen, so on a page with little content, main stretches and the footer lands at the bottom edge. On a long page, the body grows past the screen and the footer simply comes after the content, as usual. `margin: 0` removes the small margin browsers give the body by default, which would otherwise add a scrollbar to a page that exactly fits.

examples.title: A card centered on the screen
examples.prompt: A sign-in card in the middle of the screen, both ways, at any window size.
examples.code: Sign in
examples.explanation: `main` is a grid with a single cell, and `place-items: center` puts the card in the middle of that cell on both axes. `min-height: 100dvh` makes the cell as tall as the screen, so the middle is the middle of the screen, not of a cell only as tall as the card. The card's `inline-size`, its width in English, is `min(100%, 24rem)`: 24rem on a laptop, and the full width on a phone too narrow for that, with `main`'s padding keeping it off the edges. The same few lines center a loading spinner, an empty-state message, or a dialog's content.

examples.title: Logical properties in a right-to-left page
examples.prompt: A message with an icon, styled with logical properties, shown once in English and once in Arabic.
examples.code:
i Trails close at sunset.

i تغلق المسارات عند الغروب.
examples.explanation: Both paragraphs share one rule. In the English one, `border-inline-start` draws the blue bar on the left, where lines start, and `margin-inline-end` puts the icon's space on its right, between it and the words. The second paragraph has `dir="rtl"`, so its text runs from right to left: the browser puts the icon at the right end, the bar on the right edge, and the icon's space on its left, all with no extra CSS. `padding-block` and `padding-inline` are the top and bottom, then the left and right, in both. Written with `border-left` and `margin-right`, the Arabic paragraph would have its bar on the side where its lines end.

recap:
- Normal flow stacks block boxes down the page and runs inline boxes along each line, and display changes which kind a box is.
- A box with a fixed size and too much content spills out unless overflow makes it a scroll container.
- An absolute box is placed against its nearest positioned ancestor, so position: relative on a parent pins it there.
- z-index only competes inside a stacking context, so raise the group, not the child, and use dialog or popover for things that cover the page.
- Flexbox lays items along one axis: justify-content works along it, align-items across it, and flex says how items share the space.
- Grid defines rows and columns first: fr shares free space, auto-fit with minmax picks the number of columns, and named areas draw a page.
- Use Flexbox for one direction, Grid for two, and logical properties so a layout works in right-to-left languages too.
